game.name: Heroes of Hammerwatch II
game.short_description: A rogue-lite action-rpg that offers extensive persistent progression. Build your town, upgrade and equip your heroes, before taking on the ever-changing Dark Citadel - either solo or with a team of friends.

other_scores.source: TheSixthAxis (via Metacritic, only critic review, no Metascore yet)

placements.verbal_evidence: I think Heroes of Hammerrath 2 is going to be a very high B tier

commentary.label: Tier list Part 3 (2025)
commentary.summary: Heroes of Hammerwatch II is a top-down action-adventure roguelike sequel where you start in a village, push through fixed biomes (forest, cave, church, and so on) to a final boss, and rebuild the village between runs. He disliked the original somewhat but enjoyed this one enough to finish it twice. He loves the exploration, visuals, village-building meta progression and epic bosses, but finds the gameplay very simple and repetitive, with samey room-and-enemy levels. After beating the final boss he felt done. He places it at a very high B tier.
praise: Very nice, immersive visuals and environment that give a real sense of adventure
Village meta progression: new buildings and NPCs unlock new abilities after each death
Persistent character levelling with freedom to pick or switch classes at any time
Subclasses change playstyle drastically and make you much more powerful
Run-only abilities and items have cool effects and are enjoyable
Boss fights feel epic, killing huge monsters as a tiny character
Strong drive to upgrade and see the next area or boss; a solid sequel
criticism: Gameplay is extremely simple and gets repetitive, doing the same ability the same way
Levels are repetitive, mostly rooms of enemies despite good visuals
Characters and monsters are hard to see
Subclass unlocks arrive very late (about 70% through playtime)
Little reason to continue after the final boss; no hidden worlds or biomes like the first game's DLC
unique_points: Village-building meta progression gives an almost RuneScape-like feel of a persistent character
Fixed biome and boss order makes it about full exploration from village to deep final layer
Subclass system dramatically reshapes play, though gated late
commentary.quote: a very high B tier for a game that I really had an absolute blast
design_criteria: Meta-progression: village buildings, NPCs and persistent character praised as most satisfying part
Exploration/discovery: main enjoyment driver, but runs out after final boss
Visuals/atmosphere: immersive, though characters and monsters are hard to see
Gameplay depth: too simple and repetitive, same abilities used throughout
Level design: visually good but repetitive rooms of enemies
Boss design: epic feel despite simple combat
Class/subclass variety: subclass transformative but unlocked too late
Replayability/content: no hidden worlds, game feels finished after the final boss

community.one_liner: A pixel-art twin-stick action-RPG roguelite from Crackshell (published by Team17) where you build up a hub town, level seven classes and push through the Dark Citadel solo or in 4-player co-op, then grind endless New Game+ tiers.
community.consensus_summary: Players rate it Very Positive on Steam (about 82% of roughly 6,600 reviews, with the store page showing Mixed, about 69%, for the most recent 30 days), and it appears to have sold well (Boxleiter-style estimates of 1-2M owners, about $3.4M gross). The praise is for the snappy twin-stick combat, class variety, the account-wide meta-progression and co-op. The criticism is that it is light on roguelite variety (same zones in the same order), long-run balance collapses in New Game+, and content has been thin since the 1.0 launch in January 2025. Critic coverage is almost absent: Metacritic has one critic review (TheSixthAxis, 100) and no Metascore yet, and I could not find an OpenCritic page. It is fully released, not early access, and has received free updates (Epic Missions, Epic Weapons, hotfixes) plus the paid Celestial Ruins DLC with a new class. Some long-time fans now feel the developers are monetising a stagnant game.
best_things: Snappy, satisfying dual-stick combat with kiting; auto-fire skills and big lightning or piercing attacks that clear hallways of enemies feel great
Seven classes with three specialisations each; classes play distinctly and encourage experimenting
Account-wide buffs from levelling every class mean alternate characters make real progress, so you always keep something after a run
Town building and upgrades give a sticky long-term progression loop; the town is shared across characters and you keep most of your resources
Co-op for up to four players is a highlight, with easy drop-in and drop-out and the ability to leave and resume a run later; a Gauntlet-like slow-burn feel
Gorgeous pixel art, good lighting and effects, strong sound design; a solid sequel improvement over the first game's pacing
Runs are quittable and resumable at area boundaries, which suits short sessions and Steam Deck play
Responsive dev support on save problems and free post-launch updates that added missions, weapons and mode variety
worst_things: Roguelite elements are thin: the main run goes through the same zones in the same order with only tile and enemy shuffling, so runs feel alike
Late-game and New Game+ scaling breaks: enemy HP grows faster than gear and trinkets, some subclasses become too weak, and you eventually get one-shot with nothing to counter it
Content is limited after 1.0 (few bosses, maps, legendary gear); reviewers call it barebones or like an early-access game and feel 2025 roadmap promises were underdelivered
Character builds lack depth: no skill trees, upgrades are mostly flat stat increases, and loot is many tiny numerical bonuses with little identity
Save-file loss and character-deletion bugs reported by multiple players, including after updates, with some needing support tickets to restore backups
Balance issues: non-piercing weapons and single-hit defensive skills are weak at high difficulty, making some classes (e.g. Ranger) worse
Slow health and mana regeneration leaves you waiting between fights, and the screen can get cluttered by effects so you cannot read what is happening
Paid DLC (Celestial Ruins) drew anger from some players who say it should have been base-game content and that updates are scarce
improvements: More variety in tilesets, zone order, bosses and maps so runs differ more, which is the most common request
More build-defining depth: talent or skill trees, more abilities earlier, and loot with distinctive effects instead of small flat stats
Rebalance late-game and NG+ scaling so gear, trinkets and weak subclasses keep pace, and fix useless defensive skills and non-piercing weapons
Reliable cloud saves and save-loss fixes, plus an easy manual backup and copy option
Quality-of-life: faster out-of-combat regen, less visual clutter, local co-op, and more language translations (e.g. Spanish) requested on Steam forums
Deliver a larger post-launch roadmap with more maps, bosses and legendary gear
unique_things: Blends a Diablo-style ARPG with a roguelite meta-loop, built around a persistent town with NPCs and building upgrades
Account-wide class-level bonuses apply to every character, so alternate classes keep pushing your main roster forward
Dual-stick shooter-style combat with cooldown abilities, reminiscent of Gauntlet and Children of Morta
You can leave a run mid-dungeon at a level boundary and resume it later, including in multiplayer
Endless New Game+ tiers and one-time special maps unlocked through the town
Keep most resources on death (with a penalty of roughly 40% of carried gold and materials), so failure still yields progress
tedious_or_disliked: The early hours are a grind of the first zones; dozens of hours to build out the town and vendors in single-player
Re-fighting identical maps and enemies in the same positions and order across runs, including late game
Runs that turn into kiting huge mobs for long stretches once you are outscaled, with hundreds of enemies per floor on high difficulty
Waiting for health or mana to regenerate between encounters, sometimes alt-tabbing while you wait
Some permanent upgrades are per-character, so starting another class means regrinding
Control complexity for some: aiming, moving, dashing and managing several cooldowns at once (a reviewer refunded after 36 minutes)
divisive_points: Difficulty and pacing: some find it never unfair and even a bit easy, others call the early game a gear-check grind and the late game a slog
Whether it is really a roguelite: fans enjoy the slow-burn RPG progression, others say the roguelike mechanics barely matter
Value: many say it is worth the $20 and hundreds of hours, especially in co-op, while others say content runs out after 15-20 hours
Post-launch support and DLC: praised for free updates and dev responsiveness, but criticised as too sparse and monetised
community.reception_notes: Launched as a full 1.0 release on 14 Jan 2025 (Windows only, $19.99, Steam). Early reception was positive from players and TheSixthAxis gave a glowing review centred on NG+ replayability; Metacritic has only 1 critic review so no Metascore, and user score is 6.7 from 9 ratings. Steam ratings drifted: Very Positive overall but Mixed for the last 30 days as of the store page I fetched, with negative reviews in 2026 citing stagnant content, the paid Celestial Ruins DLC (new class, priced separately or in a Deluxe Edition) and lost saves after updates. The studio shipped free Epic Missions and Epic Weapons updates and hotfixes, and players mention a 2026 roadmap; some call that roadmap an undersell. Steam Deck works well per player reports, though sleep/resume can cause lag. Steam owner estimates are 1-2M and gross revenue estimates about $3.4M per steam-revenue-calculator (rough). Searches were unavailable (budget exhausted), so critic coverage beyond Metacritic could not be checked and OpenCritic was not located; Reddit was not fetchable.
